claim: RAL GTPases function in Wnt signalling-dependent intestinal stem cell proliferation and regeneration.
source: RAS-like (RAL) GTPases function in Wnt signalling-dependent intestinal stem cell proliferation and regeneration.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known finding, supported by citation to prior work (Johansson et al., 2019).

claim: RAL GTPases are necessary and sufficient to activate EGFR/MAPK signalling in the intestine via induction of EGFR internalisation.
source: Here, we show that RAL GTPases are necessary and sufficient to activate EGFR/MAPK signalling in the intestine, via induction of EGFR internalisation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript, supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures including Figure 1, Figure 4, and Figure 5.

claim: Knocking down Drosophila RalA from intestinal stem and progenitor cells leads to increased levels of plasma membrane-associated EGFR.
source: Knocking down Drosophila RalA from intestinal stem and progenitor cells leads to increased levels of plasma membrane-associated EGFR and decreased MAPK pathway activation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A, B.

claim: Knocking down Drosophila RalA from intestinal stem and progenitor cells leads to decreased MAPK pathway activation.
source: Knocking down Drosophila RalA from intestinal stem and progenitor cells leads to increased levels of plasma membrane-associated EGFR and decreased MAPK pathway activation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G, H.

claim: RAL GTPases influence stem cell proliferation during damage-induced intestinal regeneration.
source: Importantly, in addition to influencing stem cell proliferation during damage-induced intestinal regeneration, this role of RAL GTPases impacts on EGFR-dependent tumourigenic growth in the intestine and in human mammary epithelium.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 2.

claim: RAL GTPases impact EGFR-dependent tumourigenic growth in the intestine.
source: Importantly, in addition to influencing stem cell proliferation during damage-induced intestinal regeneration, this role of RAL GTPases impacts on EGFR-dependent tumourigenic growth in the intestine and in human mammary epithelium.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 5.

claim: RAL GTPases impact EGFR-dependent tumourigenic growth in human mammary epithelium.
source: Importantly, in addition to influencing stem cell proliferation during damage-induced intestinal regeneration, this role of RAL GTPases impacts on EGFR-dependent tumourigenic growth in the intestine and in human mammary epithelium.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5K, L.

claim: The effect of oncogenic RAS in the intestine is independent from RAL function.
source: However, the effect of oncogenic RAS in the intestine is independent from RAL function.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A, B.

claim: Progressive loss of control over proliferative pathways through loss of tumour suppressor genes or activation of oncogenes is associated with tumour development and progression.
source: Progressive loss of control over proliferative pathways either through loss of tumour suppressor genes or the activation of oncogenes is associated with tumour development and progression (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011.

claim: EGFR is a member of the ErbB family of growth factor receptors.
source: Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR, also known as ErbB1 or HER1) is a member of the ErbB family of growth factor receptors, which play essential roles in regulating cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival (Citri and Yarden, 2006; Wee and Wang, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Citri and Yarden, 2006 and Wee and Wang, 2017.

claim: ErbB family receptors play essential roles in regulating cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival.
source: Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR, also known as ErbB1 or HER1) is a member of the ErbB family of growth factor receptors, which play essential roles in regulating cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival (Citri and Yarden, 2006; Wee and Wang, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Citri and Yarden, 2006 and Wee and Wang, 2017.

claim: EGFR is highly expressed in intestinal stem cells and transit-amplifying cells in the mammalian intestinal epithelium.
source: In the mammalian intestinal epithelium, EGFR is highly expressed in intestinal stem cells (ISCs) and transit-amplifying cells (Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2017.

claim: EGFR ligands are released by Paneth cells and the mesenchyme.
source: EGFR ligands, such as EGF, are released by Paneth cells and the mesenchyme and are required for the maintenance and proliferation of ISCs (Dvorák et al., 1994; Jardé et al., 2020; Poulsen et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dvorák et al., 1994; Jardé et al., 2020; Poulsen et al., 1986.

claim: EGFR ligands are required for the maintenance and proliferation of intestinal stem cells.
source: EGFR ligands, such as EGF, are released by Paneth cells and the mesenchyme and are required for the maintenance and proliferation of ISCs (Dvorák et al., 1994; Jardé et al., 2020; Poulsen et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dvorák et al., 1994; Jardé et al., 2020; Poulsen et al., 1986.

claim: Ectopic activation of EGFR signalling in the intestine leads to elevated ISC proliferation.
source: Ectopic activation of EGFR signalling in the intestine by luminal application or genetic overexpression of pathway ligands (Bongers et al., 2012; Kitchen et al., 2005; Marchbank et al., 1995), or deletion of the negative regulator leucine-rich repeats and immunoglobulin-like domains protein 1 (Lrig1) (Powell et al., 2012; Wong et al., 2012), leads to elevated ISC proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bongers et al., 2012; Kitchen et al., 2005; Marchbank et al., 1995; Powell et al., 2012; Wong et al., 2012.

claim: Loss of EGFR signalling induces quiescence of Lgr5+ ISCs in vitro.
source: On the other hand, loss of EGFR signalling induces quiescence of Lgr5 + ISCs in vitro (Basak et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Basak et al., 2017.

claim: Gene amplification and activating point mutations of EGFR are highly prevalent in cancer.
source: Gene amplification and activating point mutations of EGFR are highly prevalent in cancer (Santarius et al., 2010; Yarden and Pines, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Santarius et al., 2010; Yarden and Pines, 2012.

claim: Ectopic EGFR/Ras/MAPK signalling is thought to be an early step in colorectal cancer development.
source: Ectopic EGFR/Ras/MAPK signalling is thought to be an early step in colorectal cancer (CRC) development (Calcagno et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Calcagno et al., 2008.

claim: Hyperactivation of the EGFR/Ras/MAPK pathway accelerates intestinal tumourigenesis driven by Apc loss.
source: Hyperactivation of the pathway accelerates intestinal tumourigenesis driven by Adenomatous polyposis coli loss (Apcmin/+ mice) (Luo et al., 2009), while a genetic background of partial loss-of-function of EGFR (Roberts et al., 2002) or small-molecule inhibitor treatment reduces cancer incidence (Roberts et al., 2002; Torrance et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Luo et al., 2009.

claim: Partial loss-of-function of EGFR reduces cancer incidence in Apcmin/+ mice.
source: Hyperactivation of the pathway accelerates intestinal tumourigenesis driven by Adenomatous polyposis coli loss (Apcmin/+ mice) (Luo et al., 2009), while a genetic background of partial loss-of-function of EGFR (Roberts et al., 2002) or small-molecule inhibitor treatment reduces cancer incidence (Roberts et al., 2002; Torrance et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Roberts et al., 2002.

claim: Small-molecule EGFR inhibitor treatment reduces cancer incidence in Apcmin/+ mice.
source: Hyperactivation of the pathway accelerates intestinal tumourigenesis driven by Adenomatous polyposis coli loss (Apcmin/+ mice) (Luo et al., 2009), while a genetic background of partial loss-of-function of EGFR (Roberts et al., 2002) or small-molecule inhibitor treatment reduces cancer incidence (Roberts et al., 2002; Torrance et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Roberts et al., 2002; Torrance et al., 2000.

claim: The Drosophila intestinal epithelium shares remarkable homology with its mammalian counterpart.
source: The Drosophila intestinal epithelium shares remarkable homology with its mammalian counterpart.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: The Drosophila intestine is maintained by ISCs that replenish the epithelium through progenitor cells called enteroblasts.
source: The tissue is maintained by ISCs that replenish the epithelium through progenitor cells called enteroblasts (EBs), which differentiate into either secretory enteroendocrine (EE) cells or absorptive enterocytes (ECs) (Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006; Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006; Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006.

claim: Enteroblasts differentiate into either secretory enteroendocrine cells or absorptive enterocytes.
source: The tissue is maintained by ISCs that replenish the epithelium through progenitor cells called enteroblasts (EBs), which differentiate into either secretory enteroendocrine (EE) cells or absorptive enterocytes (ECs) (Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006; Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006; Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006.

claim: Signalling pathways governing intestinal proliferation and differentiation are highly conserved between fruit flies and mammals.
source: Importantly, signalling pathways governing intestinal proliferation and differentiation are highly conserved between fruit flies and mammals (Nászai et al., 2015; Miguel-Aliaga et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nászai et al., 2015; Miguel-Aliaga et al., 2018.

claim: Activation of EGFR/Ras/MAPK within ISCs by niche-derived EGF-like ligands is essential to sustain homeostatic and regenerative proliferation of the adult fly midgut.
source: Activation of EGFR/Ras/MAPK within ISCs by niche-derived EGF-like ligands is essential to sustain homeostatic and regenerative proliferation of the adult fly midgut, while constitutive pathway activation in ISCs is sufficient to drive intestinal hyperplasia (Biteau and Jasper, 2011; Buchon et al., 2010; Jiang et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Biteau and Jasper, 2011; Buchon et al., 2010; Jiang et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2011.

claim: Constitutive EGFR/Ras/MAPK pathway activation in ISCs is sufficient to drive intestinal hyperplasia.
source: Activation of EGFR/Ras/MAPK within ISCs by niche-derived EGF-like ligands is essential to sustain homeostatic and regenerative proliferation of the adult fly midgut, while constitutive pathway activation in ISCs is sufficient to drive intestinal hyperplasia (Biteau and Jasper, 2011; Buchon et al., 2010; Jiang et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Biteau and Jasper, 2011; Buchon et al., 2010; Jiang et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2011.

claim: Regulation of EGFR signalling activity is highly dependent on various modes of receptor trafficking throughout the endocytic pathway.
source: Regulation of EGFR signalling activity is highly dependent on various modes of receptor trafficking throughout the endocytic pathway.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Abnormal trafficking of receptor tyrosine kinases is linked to cancer.
source: Indeed, abnormal trafficking of receptor tyrosine kinases is linked to cancer (Lanzetti and Di Fiore, 2017; Mosesson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lanzetti and Di Fiore, 2017; Mosesson et al., 2008.

claim: Following internalisation, EGF ligand/receptor complexes can either be targeted for recycling into the plasma membrane or ubiquitinated and targeted to late endosomes for lysosomal degradation.
source: Following internalisation through Clathrin-mediated (CME) or Clathrin-independent endocytosis (CIE) (Sorkin and Goh, 2009), EGF ligand/receptor complexes can either be targeted for recycling into the plasma membrane (PM) or ubiquitinated and targeted to late endosomes for lysosomal degradation (Sigismund et al., 2008; Sigismund et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sorkin and Goh, 2009; Sigismund et al., 2008; Sigismund et al., 2013.

claim: Autophagy has emerged as an important mechanism implicated in the termination of EGFR/MAPK signalling in the intestine.
source: Most recently, autophagy has emerged as an important mechanism implicated in the termination of EGFR/MAPK signalling in the intestine (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2019.

claim: Receptors retain their ability to relay their signal even after internalisation.
source: While endocytosis is classically considered as a process to terminate pathway activity (Tomas et al., 2014), significant evidence suggests that receptors retain their ability to relay their signal even after internalisation, hence signalling is not limited to the PM (Sadowski et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tomas et al., 2014; Sadowski et al., 2009.

claim: RAL small GTPases are best recognised for their role as effectors of Ras signalling.
source: RAL small GTPases are best recognised for their role as effectors of Ras signalling, which has attracted basic and translational research into their potential in cancer development and progression (Moghadam et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Moghadam et al., 2017.

claim: Mammalian RAL GTPases have well-characterised roles in membrane trafficking through their involvement in the exocyst complex.
source: Mammalian RAL GTPases, RALA and RALB, have well-characterised roles in membrane trafficking through their involvement in the exocyst complex (Bodemann and White, 2008; Chen et al., 2007; Chien et al., 2006) and in the regulation of Clathrin (Jullien-Flores et al., 2000) and caveolar-dependent endocytosis (Jiang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bodemann and White, 2008; Chen et al., 2007; Chien et al., 2006.

claim: Mammalian RAL GTPases have roles in the regulation of Clathrin-dependent endocytosis.
source: Mammalian RAL GTPases, RALA and RALB, have well-characterised roles in membrane trafficking through their involvement in the exocyst complex (Bodemann and White, 2008; Chen et al., 2007; Chien et al., 2006) and in the regulation of Clathrin (Jullien-Flores et al., 2000) and caveolar-dependent endocytosis (Jiang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jullien-Flores et al., 2000.

claim: Mammalian RAL GTPases have roles in the regulation of caveolar-dependent endocytosis.
source: Mammalian RAL GTPases, RALA and RALB, have well-characterised roles in membrane trafficking through their involvement in the exocyst complex (Bodemann and White, 2008; Chen et al., 2007; Chien et al., 2006) and in the regulation of Clathrin (Jullien-Flores et al., 2000) and caveolar-dependent endocytosis (Jiang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jiang et al., 2016.

claim: RAL signalling is potentiated by RALGEFs and negatively regulated by RALGAPs.
source: RAL signalling is potentiated by RALGEFs and negatively regulated by RALGAPs (Neel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Neel et al., 2011.

claim: RALGEF can be activated upon association with oncogenic RAS.
source: RALGEF, such as RALGDS, can be activated upon association with oncogenic RAS (Koyama and Kikuchi, 2001) and mediate Ras-driven skin tumourigenesis (González-García et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Koyama and Kikuchi, 2001.

claim: RALGEF mediates Ras-driven skin tumourigenesis.
source: RALGEF, such as RALGDS, can be activated upon association with oncogenic RAS (Koyama and Kikuchi, 2001) and mediate Ras-driven skin tumourigenesis (González-García et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to González-García et al., 2005.

claim: RAL GTPases have a novel role in the regulation of Wnt signalling activity in ISCs through the regulation of Wnt receptor trafficking into intracellular compartments.
source: We recently identified a novel role of RAL GTPases in the regulation of Wnt signalling activity in ISCs through the regulation of Wnt receptor trafficking into intracellular compartments (Johansson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Johansson et al., 2019.

claim: RAL function in the intestine becomes redundant upon loss of Apc.
source: The relevance of RAL GTPases in intestinal tumourigenesis remained unaddressed as their function in the intestine became redundant upon loss of Apc, a key driver of CRC (Johansson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Johansson et al., 2019.

claim: Adult wings resulting from RNAi-driven knockdown of RalA using the engrailed-gal4 driver showed a more severely dysmorphic phenotype than that caused by wingless knockdown or EGFR knockdown only.
source: We observed that adult wings resulting from RNAi-driven knockdown of RalA using the engrailed-gal4 driver (en>RalA RNAi) showed a more severely dysmorphic phenotype than that caused by wingless knockdown (en>wg RNAi) or EGFR knockdown (en>EGFR RNAi) only (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A, B.

claim: Adult wings from en>RalA RNAi animals displayed a dysmorphic phenotype similar to that resulting from combined knockdown of both wg and EGFR.
source: Instead, adult wings from en>RalA RNAi animals displayed a dysmorphic phenotype more similar to that resulting from combined knockdown of both wg and EGFR downregulation (en>wg RNAi+EGFR RNAi) (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A, B.

claim: RalA is required within ISCs to induce adult midgut regeneration following damage by oral infection with Erwinia carotovora carotovora 15.
source: RalA is required within ISCs to induce adult midgut regeneration following damage by oral infection with Erwinia carotovora carotovora 15 (Ecc15) (Johansson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Johansson et al., 2019.

claim: RalA knockdown significantly impaired damage-induced upregulation of cell cycle genes in the midgut.
source: Consistent with its effect on ISC proliferation (Johansson et al., 2019), RalA knockdown significantly impaired damage-induced upregulation of cell cycle genes in the midgut (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Levels of genes associated with the EGFR/MAPK pathway appeared increased following Ecc15 infection in control midguts in a RalA-dependent manner.
source: Additionally, levels of genes associated with the EGFR/MAPK pathway, such as argos (aos), rhomboid (rho), Sox21a, and string (stg), appeared increased following Ecc15 infection in control midguts in a RalA-dependent manner (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: RT-qPCR confirmed RNAseq results on rho, Sox21a, and stg.
source: RT-qPCR confirmed RNAseq results on rho, a well-characterised activator of EGFR/MAPK signalling in ISCs (Liang et al., 2017; Ngo et al., 2020), and two downstream targets of the pathway required for ISC proliferation, Sox21a and stg (Jin et al., 2015; Meng and Biteau, 2015; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and citations to Liang et al., 2017; Ngo et al., 2020; Jin et al., 2015; Meng and Biteau, 2015.

claim: Immunofluorescence staining for Sox21a and pERK confirmed the need for RalA for upregulation of MAPK signalling and downstream targets following damage to the midgut.
source: Furthermore, immunofluorescence staining for the transcription factor Sox21a (Meng and Biteau, 2015) and the activated form of the MAPK, phosphorylated ERK (pERK), in control animals and following RalA knockdown from ISCs/EBs confirmed the need for RalA for upregulation of MAPK signalling and downstream targets following damage to the midgut (Figure 1E–H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E–H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: Single conditional knockout of either Rala or Ralb in the murine intestinal epithelium impaired ERK activation in regenerating intestines when compared to control.
source: Single conditional knockout of either Rala (Ralafl/fl) or Ralb (Ralbfl/fl) in the murine intestinal epithelium using the Villin-CreER driver impaired ERK activation in regenerating intestines when compared to control (VillinCreER) (Figure 1I, J and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I, J and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: RAL GTPases' requirement for EGFR/MAPK pathway activation in the intestinal epithelia is evolutionarily conserved between fruit flies and mammals.
source: Therefore, RAL GTPases' requirement for EGFR/MAPK pathway activation in the intestinal epithelia is evolutionarily conserved between fruit flies and mammals.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing similar effects in both Drosophila and mouse models.

claim: Ectopic expression of wild-type RalA in ISC/EB is sufficient to induce Wnt pathway activation and intestinal proliferation in the Drosophila midgut.
source: Ectopic expression of wild-type RalA in ISC/EB is sufficient to induce Wnt pathway activation and intestinal proliferation in the Drosophila midgut (Johansson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Johansson et al., 2019.

claim: Levels of Sox21a and pERK were increased in RalA overexpressing midguts compared to wild-type control ones.
source: While levels of Sox21a and pERK were increased in RalA overexpressing midguts compared to wild-type control ones (Figure 1K–N), total levels of ERK in the midgut remained unchanged across genotypes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1K–N.

claim: Total levels of ERK in the midgut remained unchanged across genotypes following RalA overexpression.
source: While levels of Sox21a and pERK were increased in RalA overexpressing midguts compared to wild-type control ones (Figure 1K–N), total levels of ERK in the midgut remained unchanged across genotypes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, G.

claim: RAL GTPases are necessary and sufficient for EGFR/MAPK pathway activation within the intestinal epithelium.
source: Altogether, our data suggest that RAL GTPases are necessary and sufficient for EGFR/MAPK pathway activation within the intestinal epithelium.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental data showing both loss-of-function and gain-of-function effects.

claim: Small GTPases cycle between two alternative conformations: inactive (GDP-bound) and active (GTP-bound).
source: Small GTPases cycle between two alternative conformations: inactive (GDP-bound) and active (GTP-bound).
evidence: This is established knowledge about small GTPases.

claim: The balance between inactive and active states of small GTPases is determined by the activity of guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEF) and GTPase activating proteins (GAP).
source: The balance between these states is determined by the activity of guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEF) and GTPase activating proteins (GAP), which activate and inactivate GTPases, respectively (Neel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Neel et al., 2011.

claim: There are seven Ral GEFs in the human genome: RALGDS, RALGPS1-2, and RGL1-4.
source: There are seven Ral GEFs in the human genome, RALGDS, RALGPS1-2, and RGL1-4, which are often found misregulated in cancer (González-García et al., 2005; Koyama and Kikuchi, 2001; Rodriguez-Viciana and McCormick, 2005) and are considered emerging therapeutic targets (Neel et al., 2011; Vigil et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to González-García et al., 2005; Koyama and Kikuchi, 2001; Rodriguez-Viciana and McCormick, 2005; Neel et al., 2011; Vigil et al., 2010.

claim: Ral GEFs are often found misregulated in cancer.
source: There are seven Ral GEFs in the human genome, RALGDS, RALGPS1-2, and RGL1-4, which are often found misregulated in cancer (González-García et al., 2005; Koyama and Kikuchi, 2001; Rodriguez-Viciana and McCormick, 2005) and are considered emerging therapeutic targets (Neel et al., 2011; Vigil et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to González-García et al., 2005; Koyama and Kikuchi, 2001; Rodriguez-Viciana and McCormick, 2005.

claim: Ral GEFs are considered emerging therapeutic targets.
source: There are seven Ral GEFs in the human genome, RALGDS, RALGPS1-2, and RGL1-4, which are often found misregulated in cancer (González-García et al., 2005; Koyama and Kikuchi, 2001; Rodriguez-Viciana and McCormick, 2005) and are considered emerging therapeutic targets (Neel et al., 2011; Vigil et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Neel et al., 2011; Vigil et al., 2010.

claim: Several Ral GEFs are conserved in Drosophila: Rgl, GEFmeso and CG5522 (RalGPS).
source: Several Ral GEFs are conserved in Drosophila (Gentry et al., 2014): Rgl, GEFmeso and CG5522 (RalGPS).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gentry et al., 2014.

claim: Knocking down either of the three Ral GEFs significantly impaired regenerative ISC proliferation in the midgut.
source: Knocking down either of the three Ral GEFs of interest significantly impaired regenerative ISC proliferation in the midgut (Figure 2A–D) to levels comparable to those observed upon RalA knockdown (Johansson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A–D.

claim: Ral GEF knockdown led to a significant reduction in MAPK activation in the midgut following damage.
source: Furthermore, Ral GEF knockdown led to a significant reduction in MAPK activation in the midgut following damage (Figure 2E, F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E, F.

claim: Maintaining the active status of RalA is important for robust stem cell proliferation and MAPK activation in the intestine.
source: These results provide evidence highlighting the importance of maintaining the active status of RalA for robust stem cell proliferation and MAPK activation in the intestine.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on Ral GEF knockdown.

claim: Constitutive overexpression of EGFR under engrailed-gal4 caused severe organismal lethality, which was greatly suppressed by concomitant knockdown of RalA.
source: During our initial assessment of genetic interactions between EGFR signalling and RalA in adult wings, we observed that constitutive overexpression of EGFR under engrailed-gal4 (en>EGFRwt) caused severe organismal lethality, which was greatly suppressed by concomitant knockdown of RalA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Wing vein patterning defects observed in rare en>EGFRwt adult escapers was suppressed by RalA knockdown.
source: Wing vein patterning defects observed in rare en>EGFRwt adult escapers was also suppressed by RalA knockdown (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: EGFR is overexpressed in ~20% of breast and ~80% of CRCs.
source: EGFR is overexpressed in ~20% of breast and ~80% of CRCs (Rimawi et al., 2010; Spano et al., 2005), and activating mutations of Ras are one of the most common cancer-associated genetic alterations (Prior et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rimawi et al., 2010; Spano et al., 2005.

claim: Activating mutations of Ras are one of the most common cancer-associated genetic alterations.
source: EGFR is overexpressed in ~20% of breast and ~80% of CRCs (Rimawi et al., 2010; Spano et al., 2005), and activating mutations of Ras are one of the most common cancer-associated genetic alterations (Prior et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Prior et al., 2012.

claim: Activation of the EGFR/MAPK pathway in the adult Drosophila midgut by ISC/EB-specific overexpression of wild-type EGFR or constitutively active Ras was sufficient to induce intestinal hyperproliferation.
source: Activation of the EGFR/MAPK pathway in the adult Drosophila midgut by ISC/EB-specific overexpression of wild-type EGFR (EGFRWT) or constitutively active Ras (RasV12) was sufficient to induce intestinal hyperproliferation (Figure 3A, B; Jiang et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A, B and citations to Jiang et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2019.

claim: Downregulation of RalA suppressed EGFRWT- but not RasV12-driven ISC hyperproliferation.
source: Downregulation of RalA suppressed EGFRWT- but not RasV12-driven ISC hyperproliferation (Figure 3A, B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A, B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: RalA knockdown impaired activation of ERK following EGFRwt, but not RasV12 overexpression.
source: Consistently, RalA knockdown impaired activation of ERK following EGFRwt, but not RasV12 overexpression (Figure 3C, D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C, D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: Knocking down RalA significantly impaired EGFRλtop- or EGFRA887T-driven ISC proliferation.
source: However, unlike in the case of RasV12, knocking down RalA significantly impaired EGFRλtop- or EGFRA887T-driven ISC proliferation (Figure 3E, F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E, F.

claim: EGFRλtop- or EGFRA887T-dependent ERK activation was suppressed by RalA-RNAi.
source: Consistently, EGFRλtop- or EGFRA887T-dependent ERK activation was also suppressed by RalA-RNAi (Figure 3G, H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G, H.

claim: RalA influences EGFR signalling activity downstream of ligand/receptor binding.
source: These results suggest that RalA influences EGFR signalling activity downstream of ligand/receptor binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that constitutively active EGFR mutants are still sensitive to RalA knockdown.

claim: Knocking down RalA in ISCs/EBs led to significantly increased levels of PM-associated EGFR wild-type.
source: Knocking down RalA in ISCs/EBs led to significantly increased levels of PM-associated EGFR wild-type (Figure 4A, B) and A887T mutant (Figure 4C, D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A, B.

claim: Knocking down RalA in ISCs/EBs led to significantly increased levels of PM-associated EGFR A887T mutant.
source: Knocking down RalA in ISCs/EBs led to significantly increased levels of PM-associated EGFR wild-type (Figure 4A, B) and A887T mutant (Figure 4C, D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C, D.

claim: Overexpression of wild-type RalA decreased membrane localisation of EGFR.
source: Conversely, overexpression of wild-type RalA decreased membrane localisation of EGFR (Figure 4E, F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E, F.

claim: Knocking down endogenous Ras from ISCs/EBs caused a similar effect on EGFR localisation than that observed upon RalA downregulation.
source: Consistent with the role of RAL GTPases as effectors of Ras, knocking down endogenous Ras from ISCs/EBs caused a similar effect on EGFR localisation than that observed upon RalA downregulation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Activation of RalA induces EGFR/MAPK signalling in the intestine by increasing the intracellular pool of EGFR.
source: Altogether, these results strongly suggest that activation of RalA induces EGFR/MAPK signalling in the intestine by increasing the intracellular pool of EGFR.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental data on EGFR localisation and signalling.

claim: EGF-driven endocytosis of EGFR was significantly reduced by combined knockdown of Rala and Ralb in H1299 cells.
source: This clearly indicated that EGF-driven (but not EGF-independent) endocytosis of EGFR was significantly reduced by combined knockdown of Rala and Ralb (Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A, B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A, B.

claim: Integrin α5β1, transferrin, or ligand-induced c-Met receptor internalisation were not affected by Rala/b knockdown.
source: By contrast, integrin α5β1, transferrin (hTfnR), or ligand-induced c-Met receptor internalisation were not affected by Rala/b knockdown (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C–F.

claim: The effect of RAL GTPases on EGFR cellular localisation is conserved between Drosophila and mammals.
source: These results suggest that the effect of RAL GTPases on EGFR cellular localisation is conserved between Drosophila and mammals, and that RAL proteins function in a context-dependent manner, as opposed to being generally required for transmembrane or tyrosine kinase receptor trafficking dynamics.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing similar effects in both Drosophila and mammalian cells.

claim: RAL proteins function in a context-dependent manner, as opposed to being generally required for transmembrane or tyrosine kinase receptor trafficking dynamics.
source: These results suggest that the effect of RAL GTPases on EGFR cellular localisation is conserved between Drosophila and mammals, and that RAL proteins function in a context-dependent manner, as opposed to being generally required for transmembrane or tyrosine kinase receptor trafficking dynamics.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing selective effects on EGFR but not other receptors.

claim: c-Src is a conserved non-receptor tyrosine kinase whose expression is necessary and sufficient to drive regeneration and tumourigenesis of both the Drosophila and mouse intestine through EGFR/MAPK activation.
source: c-Src is a conserved non-receptor tyrosine kinase whose expression is necessary and sufficient to drive regeneration and tumourigenesis of both the Drosophila and mouse intestine through EGFR/MAPK activation (Cordero et al., 2014; Kohlmaier et al., 2015; Figure 5A, B).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cordero et al., 2014; Kohlmaier et al., 2015 and experimental data shown in Figure 5A, B.

claim: Src overexpression in ISCs/EBs induced expression of the MAPK pathway transcriptional target Sox21a.
source: Consistently, Src overexpression in ISCs/EBs (esgts>Src64wt)-induced expression of the MAPK pathway transcriptional target Sox21a (Figure 5C, D) and pERK levels (Figure 5E, F; Cordero et al., 2014; Kohlmaier et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C, D.

claim: Src overexpression in ISCs/EBs induced pERK levels.
source: Consistently, Src overexpression in ISCs/EBs (esgts>Src64wt)-induced expression of the MAPK pathway transcriptional target Sox21a (Figure 5C, D) and pERK levels (Figure 5E, F; Cordero et al., 2014; Kohlmaier et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E, F and citations to Cordero et al., 2014; Kohlmaier et al., 2015.

claim: Knocking down RalA suppressed Src-driven ISC hyperproliferation and MAPK signalling activation in the Drosophila midgut.
source: Importantly, knocking down RalA (ISC/EB>Src64wt; RalA-RNAi) suppressed Src-driven ISC hyperproliferation and MAPK signalling activation in the Drosophila midgut (Figure 5A-F), which correlated with an increase in membrane versus intracellular levels of EGFR in ISC/EB>Src64wt; RalA-RNAi midguts when compared to ISC/wt>Src64wt counterparts (Figure 5G, H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-F.

claim: Knocking down RalA in Src-overexpressing midguts correlated with an increase in membrane versus intracellular levels of EGFR.
source: Importantly, knocking down RalA (ISC/EB>Src64wt; RalA-RNAi) suppressed Src-driven ISC hyperproliferation and MAPK signalling activation in the Drosophila midgut (Figure 5A-F), which correlated with an increase in membrane versus intracellular levels of EGFR in ISC/EB>Src64wt; RalA-RNAi midguts when compared to ISC/wt>Src64wt counterparts (Figure 5G, H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G, H.

claim: T4-2 cells show robustly upregulated EGFR levels and activation.
source: Compared to the S1 predecessor, T4-2 cells grow as disorganised aggregates of cells when cultured in 3D extracellular matrix gels such as Matrigel. This growth and morphogenesis in 3D of T4-2 cells is EGFR-dependent: T4-2 show robustly upregulated EGFR levels and activation, their growth is independent of exogenous EGF, and they are acutely sensitive to EGFR inhibitors (Madsen et al., 1992; Wang et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Madsen et al., 1992; Wang et al., 1998.

claim: T4-2 cell growth is independent of exogenous EGF.
source: Compared to the S1 predecessor, T4-2 cells grow as disorganised aggregates of cells when cultured in 3D extracellular matrix gels such as Matrigel. This growth and morphogenesis in 3D of T4-2 cells is EGFR-dependent: T4-2 show robustly upregulated EGFR levels and activation, their growth is independent of exogenous EGF, and they are acutely sensitive to EGFR inhibitors (Madsen et al., 1992; Wang et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Madsen et al., 1992; Wang et al., 1998.

claim: T4-2 cells are acutely sensitive to EGFR inhibitors.
source: Compared to the S1 predecessor, T4-2 cells grow as disorganised aggregates of cells when cultured in 3D extracellular matrix gels such as Matrigel. This growth and morphogenesis in 3D of T4-2 cells is EGFR-dependent: T4-2 show robustly upregulated EGFR levels and activation, their growth is independent of exogenous EGF, and they are acutely sensitive to EGFR inhibitors (Madsen et al., 1992; Wang et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Madsen et al., 1992; Wang et al., 1998.

claim: Treating T4-2 cells with tyrphostin (AG1478) and erlotinib resulted in defective growth as determined by a reduction in 3D acinus size.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Madsen et al., 1992; Wang et al., 1998), treating T4-2 cells with two structurally independent EGFR inhibitors, tyrphostin (AG1478) and erlotinib, resulted in defective growth as determined by a reduction in 3D acinus size (Figure 5I, J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5I, J and citations to Madsen et al., 1992; Wang et al., 1998.

claim: Stable depletion of Rala or Ralb in T4-2 by shRNA phenocopied EGFR inhibition, as determined by a significant reduction in 3D acinus size.
source: Importantly, stable depletion of Rala or Ralb in T4-2 by shRNA (Figure 5K, L and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B) phenocopied EGFR inhibition, as determined by a significant reduction in 3D acinus size (Figure 5K, L).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5K, L and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: RALA/B function is required for a mammalian morphogenetic function that is dependent on EGFR.
source: Therefore, RALA/B function is similarly required for a mammalian morphogenetic function that is dependent on EGFR.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on T4-2 cells.

claim: RAL GTPases have a conserved role mediating EGFR/MAPK-dependent tissue homeostasis and transformation.
source: Altogether, our results uncover a conserved role of RAL GTPases mediating EGFR/MAPK-dependent tissue homeostasis and transformation.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental data across multiple model systems.

claim: Spatial and temporal regulation of signal transduction by the endocytic pathway plays a key role in health and pathophysiology.
source: Spatial and temporal regulation of signal transduction by the endocytic pathway plays a key role in health and pathophysiology (Casaletto and McClatchey, 2012; von Zastrow and Sorkin, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Casaletto and McClatchey, 2012; von Zastrow and Sorkin, 2007.

claim: Internalisation of membrane EGFR through Clathrin-mediated endocytosis results in prolonged EGFR signalling by favouring receptor recycling back to the PM.
source: Internalisation of membrane EGFR through Clathrin-mediated endocytosis results in prolonged EGFR signalling by favouring receptor recycling back to the PM, while Clathrin-independent endocytosis leads to EGFR degradation and signalling attenuation (Sigismund et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sigismund et al., 2008.

claim: Clathrin-independent endocytosis leads to EGFR degradation and signalling attenuation.
source: Internalisation of membrane EGFR through Clathrin-mediated endocytosis results in prolonged EGFR signalling by favouring receptor recycling back to the PM, while Clathrin-independent endocytosis leads to EGFR degradation and signalling attenuation (Sigismund et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sigismund et al., 2008.

claim: Clathrin inhibition can divert a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI)-resistant form of EGFR from Clathrin-mediated endocytosis and recycling to pinocytosis and degradation in non-small cell lung carcinoma.
source: The differential effect of endocytic trafficking on EGFR has therapeutic implications as Clathrin inhibition can divert a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI)-resistant form of EGFR from Clathrin-mediated endocytosis and recycling to pinocytosis and degradation in non-small cell lung carcinoma (Ménard et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ménard et al., 2018.

claim: The effect of knocking down RalA in the Drosophila midgut is milder than that observed upon individual or combined impairment of Wnt/β-catenin and EGFR/MAPK signalling reception in ISCs.
source: The effect of knocking down RalA in the Drosophila midgut is, however, milder than that observed upon individual or combined impairment of Wnt/β-catenin and EGFR/MAPK signalling reception in ISCs (Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2011.

claim: RalA is only partly responsible for the activation of Wnt/β-catenin and EGFR/MAPK signalling pathways.
source: This suggests that RalA is only partly responsible for the activation of these signalling pathways and its effect is only evident in the regenerative response to damage, which requires high thresholds of signalling activity to allow acute stem cell proliferation for tissue regeneration.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of phenotypes.

claim: Combined knockout of Rala and Ralb leads to complete disruption of intestinal epithelial homeostasis in the mammalian intestine.
source: The scenario is different in the mammalian intestine, where combined knockout of Rala and Ralb leads to complete disruption of intestinal epithelial homeostasis (Johansson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Johansson et al., 2019.

claim: RAL GTPases have been linked to Clathrin-mediated endocytosis via interaction of their effector protein, RAL binding protein (RALBP1), with the Clathrin adaptor AP2.
source: RAL GTPases have been linked to Clathrin-mediated endocytosis via interaction of their effector protein, RAL binding protein (RALBP1), with the Clathrin adaptor AP2 (Jullien-Flores et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jullien-Flores et al., 2000.

claim: RAL proteins have been shown to engage in Caveolin-mediated endocytosis.
source: More recently, RAL proteins have also been shown to engage in Caveolin-mediated endocytosis (Jiang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jiang et al., 2016.

claim: Excessive EGFR protein levels due to gene amplification or increased-transcription are the most common EGFR perturbations found in gastrointestinal and lung adenocarcinoma as well as in cholangiocarcinoma.
source: Excessive protein levels due to gene amplification or increased-transcription are the most common EGFR perturbations found in gastrointestinal and lung adenocarcinoma as well as in cholangiocarcinoma (Birkman et al., 2016; Jung et al., 2017; Li et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Birkman et al., 2016; Jung et al., 2017; Li et al., 2008.

claim: EGFR kinase domain activating point mutations are associated with non-small cell lung carcinoma and glioblastoma, but are rarely seen in other types of cancer.
source: On the other hand, EGFR kinase domain activating point mutations are associated with non-small cell lung carcinoma and glioblastoma, but are rarely seen in other types of cancer (Li et al., 2008; Siegelin and Borczuk, 2014; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2008; Siegelin and Borczuk, 2014; Zhang et al., 2016.

claim: Extracellular domain truncating mutations yielding to constitutively active receptor through ligand-independent dimerisation have been observed in glioblastomas.
source: Extracellular domain truncating mutations yielding to constitutively active receptor through ligand-independent dimerisation have also been observed in glioblastomas (Furnari et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2015; Huang et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Furnari et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2015; Huang et al., 1997.

claim: Genetic inhibition of Ral GTPase activity prevented hyperproliferation in models mimicking all three main classes of EGFR common to human cancers.
source: We have utilised Drosophila genetic constructs that mimic all three main classes of EGFR common to human cancers and which lead to intestinal hyperplasia when overexpressed in intestinal stem/progenitor cells (Figure 3). Genetic inhibition of Ral GTPase activity consistently prevented hyperproliferation in these models, suggesting that targeting RAL function could be a potentially effective therapeutic approach in the treatment of multiple highly aggressive cancer types.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Targeting RAL function could be a potentially effective therapeutic approach in the treatment of multiple highly aggressive cancer types.
source: We have utilised Drosophila genetic constructs that mimic all three main classes of EGFR common to human cancers and which lead to intestinal hyperplasia when overexpressed in intestinal stem/progenitor cells (Figure 3). Genetic inhibition of Ral GTPase activity consistently prevented hyperproliferation in these models, suggesting that targeting RAL function could be a potentially effective therapeutic approach in the treatment of multiple highly aggressive cancer types.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the experimental data.

claim: Current EGFR-targeted therapies include small-molecule TKIs and monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) against the extracellular domain of the receptor.
source: Current EGFR-targeted therapies include small-molecule TKIs and monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) against the extracellular domain of the receptor (Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2017.

claim: Specific kinase domain mutations desensitise cells against TKI.
source: Specific kinase domain mutations desensitise cells against TKI (Sequist et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2015), while alterations of the antibody binding site are observed in CRC (Arena et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sequist et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2015.

claim: Alterations of the antibody binding site are observed in CRC.
source: Specific kinase domain mutations desensitise cells against TKI (Sequist et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2015), while alterations of the antibody binding site are observed in CRC (Arena et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Arena et al., 2015.

claim: About 80% of CRCs are refractive to EGFR therapy.
source: The most common form of resistance to EGFR-targeted therapies is believed to be innate rather than adaptive (Parseghian et al., 2019). Indeed, about 80% of CRCs are refractive to EGFR therapy (Bardelli and Siena, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bardelli and Siena, 2010.

claim: RAL effector proteins, including RALGEFs and RALBP1, have emerged as important mediators of malignant growth in pancreatic, colorectal, prostate, bladder, and other tumour cell lines characterised by the presence of oncogenic RAS mutations.
source: RAL effector proteins, including RALGEFs and RALBP1, have emerged as important mediators of malignant growth in pancreatic, colorectal, prostate, bladder, and other tumour cell lines characterised by the presence of oncogenic RAS mutations (Neel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Neel et al., 2011.

claim: Genetic knockout of the RALGEF, RALGDS, ameliorates tumour growth in a mouse model of Ras-driven skin tumourigenesis.
source: Furthermore, genetic knockout of the RALGEF, RALGDS, ameliorates tumour growth in a mouse model of Ras-driven skin tumourigenesis (González-García et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to González-García et al., 2005.

claim: Fly and murine intestines bearing loss of Apc overcome the need for RAL GTPases to proliferate.
source: Previously, we have shown that fly and murine intestines bearing loss of Apc, a key initiating event in up to 80% of human CRC, also overcome the need for RAL GTPases to proliferate (Johansson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Johansson et al., 2019.

claim: Anti-RAL therapies are unlikely to be effective to treat CRCs carrying Apc loss-of-function and/or hyperactivating Ras mutations.
source: Taken together, our results argue against an effective role of anti-RAL therapies to treat CRCs carrying Apc loss-of-function and/or hyperactivating Ras mutations.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing independence from RAL function in these contexts.

claim: Tumours with overexpression or activating mutations in EGFR might be responsive to impairment of RAL function.
source: On the other hand, tumours with overexpression or activating mutations in EGFR, such as carcinomas of the upper gastrointestinal tract, lung and mammary tissue, or glioblastomas (Birkman et al., 2016; Furnari et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2015; Huang et al., 1997; Li et al., 2008; Siegelin and Borczuk, 2014; Zhang et al., 2016), might be responsive to impairment of RAL function.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the experimental data and citations to Birkman et al., 2016; Furnari et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2015; Huang et al., 1997; Li et al., 2008; Siegelin and Borczuk, 2014; Zhang et al., 2016.
